newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Tutsi rebels hold Bukavu, U.N. demands ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Tutsi rebels hold Bukavu, U.N. demands ceasefire.

text.p: Tutsi rebels control Zaire's eastern town of Bukavu and diplomats say troops from Tutsi-led Rwanda have been seen in Goma, the Zairean army's main base in the region.
The U.N. Security Council on Friday demanded a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and called on the international community to come up with an urgent response to the crisis.
The United States threw its weight behind a regional conference due to be held in Nairobi next Tuesday which is expected to discuss the conflict.

News from the battle-front, though confused, suggested that Zaire's ragged army and allied Rwandan Hutu fighters faced the prospect of defeat by well-armed rebels in both North and South Kivu, the two eastern provinces facing Rwanda and Burundi.
In Zaire's capital Kinshasa, Tutsis, who feature prominently in the city's business and professional classes, started to pack and flee, fearing a witchhunt following fighting in the east.

"There are RPA (Rwandan Patriotic Army) troops in uniforms in the centre of Goma city, the main square. They came in by land and across Lake Kivu on boats landing on the city beach," said one diplomat in the region, quoting witnesses.
"We are 110 percent certain the RPA is in Goma. It is confirmed," said another diplomat.
Hutu-Tutsi rivalry and hatred has poisoned life in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi for generations.
Over a million Hutu refugees have lived in camps in eastern Zaire since 1994 when they fled Rwanda fearing reprisals or an upsurge in civil war after the genocide of Tutsis there.
Rwanda denies having any troops in Goma but says it reserves the right to defend itself from cross-border shelling.

Cross-border exchanges between Rwanda and Zaire complicated plans by the U.N. to pull out staff from Goma, centre for efforts to help 1.1 million Rwandan refugees, 200,000 Burundians and tens of thousands of Zaireans uprooted by the fighting.
Well-equipped rebels, who politely explain their presence and ask civilians to stay, seized Bukavu on Wednesday.

The town was quiet on Friday. Some civilians who fled the rebel advance started to trickle back. The town has had no electricity since Tuesday. A large number of foreigners are staying in a religious compound.
The rebels appear well-disciplined and well-organised, unlike Zairean troops who looted aid agencies and civilian homes in the last few days of fighting.
Rebel commanders say they are Zairean and speak a variety of languages including Swahili, Lingala, French and English.
Zaire says Rwandan, Burundian and Ugandan soldiers are fighting alongside the rebels.

Hundreds of Zaireans stayed in the town during the fighting and some ethnic Tutsis, who said they were hiding, emerged and reported killings by Rwandan Hutu militiamen and people with clubs and machetes.

In Kinshasa, Zaire's transitional parliament called on Thursday for Tutsis to be sacked from the army, civil service and state-run firms. On Friday, a mob of several hundred Zairean youths attacked Tutsi-owned property in the capital.
Hundreds of Tutsis have already quit Kinshasa, most fleeing across the broad Zaire River to Congo. Many talk of harassment.

Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, his government under pressure over the fighting in the east, said Zaire's army had retaken Bukavu and Uvira to the south, where the rebels launched their revolt a fortnight ago.
Kengo, who is part Tutsi, said Zaire's army had the means to defend the country. "Nobody can say that the army doesn't have the means for its operation," he said.
The U.N. Security Council said there was an "urgent need for a comprehensive and coordinated response by the international community to prevent any further escalation of the crisis".
A statement read by council president Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia said all nations should respect "the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of their neighbours.

U.N. General Assembly president Razali Ismail of Malaysia voiced frustration over the crisis, saying he had reached the "horrible conclusion that we are unable collectively or individually to do enough to prevent the human tragedies before us".

Kenyan state radio said on Thursday leaders of Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Cameroon had been invited to a conference in Nairobi next Tuesday, although it did not specifically spell out that Zaire would be the main topic.

"The United States supports this call for a regional conference," said U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, adding that it would include the United Nations and interested Western countries including the United States.
